title: CFA Ethics 8: In-depth case studies - Standard VI & VII
subtitle: Conflicts of Interest and Responsibilities as a CFA Member or Candidate
whyItMatters: Standard VI (conflicts of interest) and Standard VII (responsibilities to the CFA programme) close out the seven Standards - and Standard VII matters to you personally if you are a CFA candidate, because it governs your own conduct in the exam.
openingQuestion: A financial adviser recommends an investment-linked insurance product to a client without disclosing that he receives a 15% commission on the contract value from the insurer - far higher than the commission on other products. What does this breach?
openingOptions: No breach, since sales commissions are entirely normal in the finance industry
A breach of Standard VI(A) - every conflict must be disclosed
A breach only if the product genuinely does not suit the client
A breach of Standard V, because it concerns investment analysis
explanation: This breaches Standard VI(A) - Disclosure of Conflicts. The problem is not receiving a commission, which is common and not wrong in itself, but FAILING TO DISCLOSE a materially skewed commission structure. A client is entitled to know the financial incentive behind a recommendation so they can judge its objectivity for themselves - whether or not the product ultimately turns out to suit them.

realWorldExample.description: The distinction between a fee-only adviser (paid a fixed fee by the client, taking no product commission) and a commission-based one (paid per product sold) is Standard VI showing up in the structure of the industry itself. Many professional bodies encourage the fee-only model precisely because it minimises the conflicts that would otherwise need disclosing - though both models can operate ethically where the disclosure obligation is met in full.

quiz.question: What order of priority does Standard VI(B) - Priority of Transactions set when a manager trades for both clients and a personal account?
options: Only applies if the personal trade is over 10% of the client's
The personal account always goes ahead of the client's orders
Client trades must come before or alongside personal ones
There is no specific rule about the order transactions go in
quiz.explanation: Standard VI(B) requires trades for clients and prospective clients to come before, or at the same time as, trades for the manager's own account or that of a related person. There is no size threshold that switches the rule on - it applies to every personal trade. The principle stops a manager front-running an attractive opportunity for themselves before allocating it to clients, which is precisely the reversal the second option describes.

quiz.question: What does Standard VI(C) - Referral Fees require when an adviser refers a client to another service, such as a different asset manager, in exchange for a fee?
options: Referral fees are prohibited outright in all circumstances
Disclosure is needed only if the fee exceeds a set threshold
No disclosure needed where the referred firm is reputable
The client must be told about that referral fee
quiz.explanation: In line with the general philosophy of Standard VI, referral fees are not banned but must be disclosed. The client needs to know the referral carries a financial incentive so they can judge how objective the advice really is. No monetary threshold exists below which the obligation lapses, and the quality of the firm being referred to is beside the point: a reputable destination does not make the adviser's incentive any less relevant to the client's assessment.

quiz.question: What conduct by a CFA candidate does Standard VII(A) - Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs cover?
options: All conduct around the CFA programme: enrolment, the exam, and afterwards
Only once you have formally become a CFA charterholder yourself
Not to candidates at all, only to the invigilators present in the hall
Only while you are actually sitting the paper in the exam hall
quiz.explanation: Standard VII(A) is broad and protects the integrity of the whole CFA programme - from enrolment (no false information on your application), through the exam itself (no cheating), to afterwards (no disclosure of exam content you undertook to keep confidential). Candidates are squarely within its scope, not only charterholders and certainly not only invigilators, and it does not switch off when you leave the hall. A breach at any stage can void your result or bar you permanently.

quiz.question: What does Standard VII(B) - Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program allow a candidate who has not passed all three levels to say about themselves?
options: It applies to business cards only, and never to social media posts
You may only state your true status, such as 'CFA Level II Candidate'
You may not mention sitting the CFA exams in any form at all
You may call yourself 'CFA' as soon as you register for Level I
quiz.explanation: Standard VII(B) requires a candidate to describe their position in the programme accurately - using a phrase such as 'CFA Level II Candidate' only when you have actually passed Level I and are validly registered for Level II, and never implying you hold the charter before completing all three levels plus the work experience requirement. Mentioning the programme is entirely permitted, so long as the description is true. And the rule follows the claim wherever it appears, on a business card or a LinkedIn profile alike.

quiz.question: What order of priority does Standard VI(B) require when transactions are executed?
options: Whoever placed the order first is filled first, whatever the account type
The firm first, then clients, and employee accounts last of all
Clients first, then the firm, and the personal account last
The account with the larger asset base gets its order filled first
quiz.explanation: The Standard does not prohibit employees trading for themselves, but it puts them at the back of the queue. The reason is specific: trading ahead of a client lets you profit from the price move the client's own order is about to cause - the hardest kind of conflict for an outsider to detect. Filling in the order received, or by account size, would leave that route wide open, and putting the firm ahead of clients inverts the fiduciary relationship entirely.

keyTakeaways: Standard VI(A) does not prohibit conflicts from existing; it requires transparent disclosure so the client can judge for themselves
Standard VI(B) requires client trades always to come before or alongside the manager's personal trades
Standard VII(A) protects the integrity of the entire CFA programme, from enrolment through the exam and afterwards
Standard VII(B) requires candidates to describe their status accurately, never implying they hold the charter before qualifying

practicePrompt.question: Which of the following is correct according to this lesson?
options: Standard VI prohibits every form of commission and referral fee across all of finance
Standard VI(B) requires client trades to come before or alongside the manager's own
A CFA candidate may call themselves 'CFA' as soon as they register for Level I
Standard VII(A) applies only in the exam hall, not at enrolment or afterwards
practicePrompt.explanation: Standard VI(B) requires trades for clients to be executed before, or at the same time as, trades for the manager's personal account. The other three each reverse something the lesson establishes: Standard VI is built on disclosure rather than prohibition, the charter may only be claimed after all three levels plus the experience requirement, and Standard VII(A) covers the whole programme from enrolment onwards.

summary.keyIdea: Standard VI handles conflicts of interest through transparent disclosure and client priority, while Standard VII protects the integrity of the CFA programme you are studying in yourself
summary.commonMistake: Assuming that taking a commission or a referral fee is automatically unethical - the real issue is whether it was disclosed transparently, not the fee itself.
summary.action: As a CFA candidate, audit yourself: are you describing your exam status accurately on your profile, your social media, and your CV?

application.title: Audit your own candidate status
application.message: If you are sitting or plan to sit the CFA exams, review how you describe your progress on LinkedIn and your CV - make sure the wording matches reality (say 'CFA Level I Candidate' only once you are validly registered, not merely intending to sit).
application.secondary: This is the most direct and concrete application of Standard VII(B) to your own CFA journey.

sections.text: Standards VI and VII close out the seven Standards of Professional Conduct - Standard VI handles the many shapes a conflict of interest takes in finance, while Standard VII bears directly on you if you are working through the CFA exams.
VI(A) and VI(C): disclose, do not prohibit

A common misreading is that Standard VI bans conflicts of interest outright. In fact its central philosophy is TRANSPARENT DISCLOSURE rather than absolute prohibition - because many conflicts, such as product commissions and referral fees, are a normal part of doing business in finance. What matters is that the client is fully informed and can judge the objectivity of the advice they are receiving.
VI(B): who gets first bite at a good opportunity?

Priority of Transactions addresses one very concrete problem: when an attractive opportunity appears, such as an IPO allocation, the manager must not let their own or their family's account get in ahead of client accounts. The principle is that clients always come first, or at worst at the same time, as the personal interest of the person managing their money.

sections.label: In practice: fee-only versus commission-based
sections.text: The advice industry distinguishes two models: fee-only (paid a fixed or hourly fee by the client) and commission-based (paid out of the products sold). Both can operate ethically if Standard VI is fully observed, but the fee-only model inherently carries fewer conflicts to disclose - which is why many professionals suggest investors seek out a fee-only adviser where they can.
VII: your responsibility to the programme you are studying

Standard VII(A) protects the integrity of the whole CFA programme - from enrolment (no false claims about background or experience), through the exam (no cheating, no prohibited materials), to afterwards (no disclosure of exam content you undertook to keep confidential). Standard VII(B) is very specific and very practical: describe your position in the programme ACCURATELY - use 'CFA Level II Candidate' only when you have actually passed Level I and qualify to register for Level II, and never imply you hold the charter before you have completed everything required.

items: Standard VI(A): disclose the conflict of interest; it is not an outright prohibition
Standard VI(B): clients always come before, or at the same time as, the manager's personal account
Standard VI(C): referral fees must be disclosed, but taking one is not prohibited
Standard VII(A): protects the whole CFA programme from enrolment through to after the exam
Standard VII(B): describe your candidate status accurately, never implying a charter you have not earned

lines: With eight Ethics lessons behind you (the Code of Ethics, the seven Standards in overview, four in-depth case study lessons on each pair, and GIPS), you have a solid enough base to handle most Ethics questions on the CFA Level I exam with confidence.
Ethics is the subject that most rewards repeated revision - come back to these case studies periodically before exam day.
